name: Antony of Egypt
sketch: Antony was a well-off young Egyptian who gave away his inheritance, lived alone among the tombs and then in a ruined fort, and became the father of Christian monks. We know him mainly through the Life that Athanasius wrote soon after his death. Dates for the early part are traditional: the Life gives few years, so they are marked "c." here.

events.text: The emperor Decius orders everyone in the empire to offer sacrifice; the first empire-wide persecution of Christians begins around the time of Antony's birth. Context from settled history.
Antony is born, traditionally about this year, at Coma in Upper Egypt, to Christian parents of good family and some wealth.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 1
step.quote: Antony you must know was by descent an Egyptian: his parents were of good family and possessed considerable wealth
step.note: Athanasius gives no year of birth. The date is a later estimate worked back from his reported age of about 105 at death.

events.text: With both parents dead, he is left to care for a young sister. Hearing the Gospel read in church, he sells the family land, provides for her, and gives the rest to the poor.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 2
step.quote: After the death of his father and mother he was left alone with one little sister: his age was about eighteen or twenty
step.note: The Life puts him at eighteen or twenty at the start of his new way of life. The editors of the bundled translation place this about 271.

events.text: He learns discipline from the good men around the village, copying one man's prayer, another's gentleness and another's patience.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 4
step.quote: He observed the graciousness of one; the unceasing prayer of another; he took knowledge of another's freedom from anger and another's loving-kindness
step.note: He does not invent a new way; he learns from the holy people already near him.

events.text: The devil assails him with memories of wealth, family and ease. Later, shut in a tomb, he is beaten so badly that friends carry him away as if dead. He asks to be taken back to the tomb.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 8
step.quote: he so cut him with stripes that he lay on the ground speechless from the excessive pain
step.note: Athanasius does not date this. The Life says the trial came in the tombs near his village, soon after he began.

events.text: Crossing the Nile, he takes up residence in a deserted fort and stays shut in there for about twenty years, seeing almost no one. Bread is lowered to him twice a year.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 12
step.quote: Thus he employed a long time training himself, and received loaves, let down from above, twice in the year.
step.note: The bundled translation guesses 285 for the move to the fort; the Life says "nearly twenty years" in solitude.

events.text: Diocletian begins the Great Persecution: churches are destroyed, Scriptures burned, clergy imprisoned. It lasts in the East until about 311. Context from settled history.
Friends break down the door. Antony comes out calm and unchanged, heals many, and becomes the guide of a growing number who want to live as he does.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 14
step.quote: Antony, as from a shrine, came forth initiated in the mysteries and filled with the Spirit of God.
step.note: This is the traditional start of organised monastic life in Egypt.

events.text: He teaches the assembled monks. The Life gives his address, which begins by telling them that the Scriptures are enough for instruction.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 16
step.quote: The Scriptures are enough for instruction
step.note: The address is given as a speech in Egyptian, rendered into Greek by Athanasius.

events.text: During the persecution Antony goes to Alexandria hoping to be martyred. When the persecution ends he returns to his cell, still serving the confessors.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 46
step.quote: After this the Church was seized by the persecution
step.note: The section title in the bundled text dates this visit to the persecution of 311.

events.text: The Edict of Milan grants Christians legal toleration across the empire. Context from settled history.
The Council of Nicaea condemns Arius and confesses the Son "of one substance" with the Father. Context from settled history.
Emperor Constantine and his sons write to Antony as to a father. He is unimpressed and tells the monks that it is more wonderful that God has written to us.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 81
step.quote: Constantine Augustus, and his sons Constantius and Constans the Augusti wrote letters to him, as to a father
step.note: Constantine died in 337, so the letters come before that; the Life gives no exact year.

events.text: When the Arians claim Antony agrees with them, he comes down from the mountain to Alexandria and publicly denounces them. Crowds, including many pagans, come to see him.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 69
step.quote: he descended from the mountain, and having entered Alexandria
step.note: A note in the bundled text gives July 338 for the visit.

events.text: Aged about 105, he tells the brethren that his end is near and urges them to avoid the Arians and the Meletian schismatics.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 89
step.quote: At length the time of my departure is at hand, for I am near a hundred and five years old.
step.note: The Life gives his age but not the year of death. The Introduction of the bundled text puts it in 356.

events.text: He dies on the inner mountain and is buried in secret, as he had asked, so that his body would not be kept in a house as was the Egyptian custom.

step.label: Athanasius, Life of Antony 92
step.quote: he lifted up his feet, and as though he saw friends coming to him and was glad because of them
step.note: Athanasius adds that no one but two companions knew the place of burial.

name: Ambrose of Milan
sketch: Ambrose was a Roman governor who was chosen bishop of Milan by acclamation before he was even baptized. He stood against Arian emperors, defended the Church's freedom, led the people in song, and taught the young Augustine to read Scripture in the Spirit.

events.text: Ambrose is born about this year, the son of a Roman official in Gaul.

step.label: Butler, St. Ambrose
step.quote: The saint's birth happened about the year 340.
step.note: Butler gives only an approximate year, and says authors disagree about the city.

events.text: He trains as an advocate and becomes known for pleading cases at the court of the praetorian prefect Probus, who makes him his assessor. He is later made governor of the province that includes Milan.

step.label: Butler, St. Ambrose
step.quote: in his court St Ambrose pleaded causes with so much reputation
step.note: Butler dates Probus's office to 368.

events.text: The Milan church is torn between Arians and Catholics after the Arian bishop dies. Ambrose, governor and still only a catechumen, is acclaimed bishop. He is baptized and consecrated on 7 December.

step.label: Butler, St. Ambrose
step.quote: the 7th of December in 374, not in 375
step.note: Butler corrects some authors who gave 375.

events.text: At the request of the young emperor Gratian he writes On the Faith against the Arians, adding more books in 379.

step.label: Butler, St. Ambrose
step.quote: the holy prelate wrote, in 377, the work entitled, On the Faith, to Gratian
step.note: Butler gives 377 for the first books and 379 for the later ones.

events.text: The Gothic victory at Adrianople kills the eastern emperor Valens and shocks the empire. Context from settled history.

The prefect Symmachus asks that the altar of Victory be restored to the Senate House. Ambrose writes to the emperor Valentinian II to refuse. In the same year a young teacher of rhetoric named Augustine arrives in Milan and goes to hear him.

step.label: Ambrose, Letter 18
step.quote: Since the illustrious Symmachus, Prefect of the city, has sent petition to your Grace that the altar, which was taken away from the Senate House of the city of Rome, should be restored to its place
step.note: Ambrose replies to the Memorial of Symmachus, which is bundled with the letter.

events.text: Augustine writes of reaching Milan: Ambrose is "known to the whole world as among the best of men".

step.label: Augustine, Confessions V
step.quote: To Milan I came, to Ambrose the Bishop, known to the whole world as among the best of men
step.note: Augustine later credits Ambrose's preaching with opening Scripture to him.

events.text: The empress Justina, an Arian, demands a basilica for her party. Ambrose refuses and the people keep watch in the church with him for days. He writes to his sister about it.

step.label: Ambrose, Letter 20
step.quote: I replied, of course, that the temple of God could not be surrendered by a Bishop.
step.note: The bundled translation heads this letter "Easter, a.d. 385"; many scholars date it Easter 386. The year is uncertain.

events.text: He finds the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and moves them to his new basilica, just as the quarrel over churches is at its sharpest.

step.label: Ambrose, Letter 22
step.quote: you must know that we have found some bodies of holy martyrs
step.note: He tells the discovery to his sister Marcellina.

events.text: At the Easter vigil he baptizes Augustine, Alypius and Augustine's son Adeodatus.

step.label: Augustine, Confessions IX
step.quote: and we were baptised, and anxiety for our past life vanished from us
step.note: Augustine says the baptism took away his anxiety about his past life.

events.text: After the Emperor Theodosius has thousands killed at Thessalonica, Ambrose writes that he dare not offer the sacrifice if the emperor is present. Theodosius submits to public penance.

step.label: Ambrose, Letter 51
step.quote: I dare not offer the sacrifice if you intend to be present.
step.note: Butler dates the council on this subject to 390 and says Theodosius spent eight months in penance.

events.text: Theodosius dies at Milan; the empire is divided between his sons Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West. Context from settled history.
Told that Milan will suffer if he dies, Ambrose answers that he is not ashamed to have lived among them and is not afraid to die. He dies in early April.

step.label: Butler, St. Ambrose
step.quote: I have not so behaved myself among you that I should be ashamed to live longer ; nor am I afraid to die, because we have a good master.
step.note: Butler follows Paulinus, his secretary, who was present.

name: Basil the Great
sketch: Basil grew up in a Christian family in Cappadocia, studied in Athens with his friend Gregory, and left a career in teaching to live as a monk. As bishop of Caesarea he fed the poor, stood up to an Arian emperor's officials and wrote on the Holy Spirit and the monastic life. Much of what we know of him comes from Gregory of Nazianzus's funeral oration.

events.text: Basil is born towards the end of 329 at Caesarea in Cappadocia, into a family that had already suffered for the faith.

step.label: Butler, St. Basil
step.quote: was born towards the close of the year 329
step.note: Butler's dating; the OCR of the bundled Butler is rough, but the year is clear.

events.text: At Athens he meets his old Cappadocian acquaintance Gregory again. They become the closest of friends, known only by the road to church and the road to the schools.

step.label: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43
step.quote: We were contained by Athens, like two branches of some river-stream
step.note: Gregory's funeral oration for Basil is the main source for their student years. Butler dates Gregory's meeting with Basil at Athens to 352.

events.text: Back in Caesarea, he opens a school of rhetoric. His fame as a speaker grows quickly and the city treats him as its second founder.

step.label: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43
step.quote: The city of Cæsarea took possession of him, as a second founder and patron
step.note: Gregory describes the return from Athens and the pull of public life. Basil soon grows uneasy about it.

events.text: Convinced his own life is empty, he tours the monasteries and hermitages of Syria, Mesopotamia and Egypt to learn how the best of them live.

step.label: Butler, St. Basil
step.quote: in 357 travelled over Syria, Mesopotamia, and Egypt, and visited the most celebrated monasteries
step.note: Butler dates the journey to 357.

events.text: He settles on his family estate in Pontus, on the river Iris, and writes frankly to Gregory that his troubles came with him.

step.label: Basil, Letter 2
step.quote: I have abandoned my life in town, as one sure to lead to countless ills; but I have not yet been able to get quit of myself.
step.note: The bundled letter is placed about 358. Basil admits that a change of place does not change the heart.

events.text: Julian, who had once studied at Athens with Basil and Gregory, becomes emperor and tries to restore the old pagan worship. Context from settled history.
His bishop, Eusebius, ordains him priest. Soon they quarrel, and Basil withdraws again to Pontus until the bishop is reconciled to him.

step.label: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43
step.quote: There arose a disagreement between him and his predecessor
step.note: Gregory gives no date. Butler places Basil's ordination as priest in 363.

events.text: The brothers Valentinian and Valens become emperors. Valens rules the East and backs the Arian party. Context from settled history.
In a time of famine he spends his own wealth on grain and soup for the poor. Gregory calls him a second Joseph.

step.label: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43
step.quote: Such was our young furnisher of corn, and second Joseph
step.note: Gregory gives no year. The great Cappadocian famine is usually placed about 368; Butler mentions an earlier famine around 359, so the date here is only approximate.

events.text: When Eusebius dies, Basil is chosen and consecrated archbishop of Caesarea, a church that governs most of the province.

step.label: Butler, St. Basil
step.quote: the saint was chosen and consecrated archbishop of that metropolitical church
step.note: Butler dates this to the middle of 370.

events.text: The prefect Modestus threatens him with confiscation, exile, torture and death if he will not accept the Arian creed. Basil answers that a man with only a few books and torn clothes has nothing to lose.

step.label: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43
step.quote: No one has ever yet spoken thus, and with such boldness, to Modestus.
step.note: Gregory reports the exchange. The year 372 is the usual modern dating; the bundled text gives none.

events.text: The Arian emperor Valens is killed by the Goths at Adrianople on 9 August, and Gratian restores peace to the Church.

step.label: Butler, St. Basil
step.quote: on the 9th of August, 378, peace was restored to the church by the emperor Gratian
step.note: Butler dates the death of Valens to 9 August 378.

events.text: Basil dies on 1 January, worn out at about fifty. Gregory says the whole city poured out around him. Gregory cannot attend because of illness and writes the funeral oration later.

step.label: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43
step.quote: He lay, drawing his last breath, and awaited by the choir on high
step.note: The editor's note in the bundled text gives the date of death as 1 January 379.

events.text: The Council of Constantinople confirms the Nicene faith, including the full divinity of the Holy Spirit that Basil had defended. Context from settled history.

name: Gregory of Nazianzus
sketch: Gregory was a bishop's son who wanted only a quiet life of study and prayer, and was dragged again and again into church office. He was Basil's closest friend, a poet and preacher, and for a short time the bishop of Constantinople who won back the city's Catholics. He gave up the see at the Council of 381 and went home.

events.text: Born at Arianzum near Nazianzus in Cappadocia to Nonna and a convert father who later became bishop. His mother had prayed hard for a son and offered him to God at his birth.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: Gregory was the fruit of the most earnest prayers of his mother, who, upon his birth, offered him to God
step.note: Butler gives no birth year here. About 329-330 is the usual estimate.

events.text: Sailing to Athens for study, he is caught in a storm for twenty days and, still unbaptized, promises to give his life to God if he survives.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: God was pleased to hear his prayer : the tempest ceased
step.note: Butler gives no year; this is the traditional account from Gregory's own writings. The date is approximate.

events.text: At Athens he meets Basil again. Their friendship becomes the model of holy friendship.

step.label: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 43
step.quote: We were contained by Athens, like two branches of some river-stream
step.note: Gregory looks back on the friendship in his funeral oration for Basil.

events.text: The future emperor Julian comes to Athens. Gregory sizes him up and fears what kind of ruler he will be.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: In 355, Julian, afterwards emperor, came to Athens
step.note: Butler reports Gregory's early misgivings about Julian.

events.text: Gregory joins Basil in his retreat on the river Iris in Pontus for prayer, psalmody, Scripture and manual work.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: He accordingly, in 358, joined St. Basil in the solitude into which he had retreated
step.note: Butler adds that Gregory enjoyed this solitude only briefly before his father called him home.

events.text: His father, then over eighty, ordains him priest by surprise. Gregory flees to Pontus, then comes back at Easter after about ten weeks.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: To draw the greater succor from him he ordained him priest by force, and when he least expected it.
step.note: Butler says the ordination was probably on Christmas Day, 361. Gregory's speech defending his flight is the first of his Orations.

events.text: Julian becomes sole emperor and tries to restore pagan worship. Context from settled history.
Basil, needing allies in a contested diocese, makes Gregory bishop of Sasima, a poor staging post. Gregory is never able to take up the place, and feels used by his friend.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: He appointed our saint bishop of Sasima, a small town in that division.
step.note: Butler tells the story; the year 372 is the usual date and is not given in this passage.

events.text: His father dies in 374, above ninety years of age, after about forty-five years as bishop of Nazianzus. Gregory had been helping to run the diocese.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: which he held about forty-five years, dying in 374, when he was above ninety years old
step.note: Butler dates the death of the elder Gregory to 374.

events.text: The Arian emperor Valens is killed at Adrianople; the new ruler Theodosius backs the Nicene faith. Context from settled history.
A few Nicene Christians invite him to Constantinople, where the Arians hold all the churches. He preaches in a relative's house and calls it Anastasia, the Resurrection.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: He soon after converted it into a church, and gave it the name of Anastasia, or the Resurrection
step.note: Butler describes the small Catholic community that grew around him.

events.text: A Cynic philosopher named Maximus, with Egyptian bishops behind him, has himself secretly consecrated bishop of Constantinople. Theodosius throws him out, and Gregory is installed in the great church.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: procured himself to be ordained bishop of Constantinople, in a clandestine manner
step.note: Butler describes the intrigue. Gregory's five Theological Orations belong to these years.

events.text: The bishops at the Council of Constantinople turn on him over who should hold the see. Gregory preaches a farewell and resigns.

step.label: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 42
step.quote: Give me a respite from my long labours
step.note: The bundled translation says the farewell was spoken during the Second Ecumenical Council in 381.

events.text: Back in Cappadocia, he arranges a bishop for Nazianzus and keeps up his writing in retirement, including poems. In Lent 382 he keeps forty days of complete silence.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: he, in 382, passed the forty days of Lent in absolute silence
step.note: Butler reports the Lenten silence in 382.

events.text: Gregory dies in 389, or 391 according to some. Later tradition names him "the Theologian"; the Church honors him as one of the Cappadocian Fathers.

step.label: Butler, St. Gregory Nazianzen
step.quote: his happydeath in 389, or, according to others, in 391
step.note: Butler leaves the year open between 389 and 391.

name: Cyprian of Carthage
sketch: Cyprian was a well-educated Carthaginian lawyer and teacher who was baptized as an adult, made bishop within two years, and then led his church through persecution, plague and a bitter quarrel over the lapsed and over baptism. His deacon Pontius wrote the account of his death.

events.text: Cyprian is born, probably about this year, to a respectable family in Carthage, and trained as a rhetorician.

step.label: Introductory Notice to Cyprian
step.quote: born probably about 200 a.d.
step.note: The editor says the date is only a probable one, and that little is certain about his early life.

events.text: Through his friend, the presbyter Caecilius, he is brought from his worldly errors to Christ. At baptism he takes his friend's name. His first letter, to Donatus, was written soon after.

step.label: Pontius, Life and Passion of Cyprian 4
step.quote: who had converted him from his worldly errors to the acknowledgment of the true divinity
step.note: The Introductory Notice dates his conversion to 246.

events.text: Still a new Christian, he is chosen bishop of Carthage by the people, against the wishes of some of the older presbyters.

step.label: Introductory Notice to Cyprian
step.quote: the popular urgency constrained him to accept the office of Bishop of Carthage
step.note: The Notice gives 248 for his election.

events.text: Decius becomes emperor and the next year orders every citizen to offer sacrifice. Context from settled history.
When the Decian persecution breaks out, Cyprian goes into hiding and directs the church by letter. The Roman clergy sharply criticize him for leaving.

step.label: Introductory Notice to Cyprian
step.quote: induced Cyprian to retire into concealment for a time
step.note: Pontius defends the withdrawal as God's will; Cyprian's critics saw it as flight.

events.text: Many fall away under pressure. Cyprian writes to the lapsed, who write back humbly, and works out how and when they can be restored.

step.label: Cyprian, Epistle 26
step.quote: some who are of the lapsed have lately written to me, and are humble and meek and trembling and fearing God
step.note: The bundled text dates the letter 250.

events.text: Back in Carthage, he writes On the Unity of the Church against the schismatic groups that had grown up. It contains his best-known line about the Church as mother.

step.label: Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church
step.quote: He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother.
step.note: The date 251 is the usual one and is not given in this passage.

events.text: A plague sweeps through Carthage. Pagans abandon the sick and dying in the street. Cyprian organizes the Christians to care for them, friend or enemy.

step.label: Pontius, Life and Passion of Cyprian 9
step.quote: Afterwards there broke out a dreadful plague
step.note: Pontius gives no year. Modern historians usually place the plague about 252.

events.text: A council of African bishops decides that people baptized by heretics must be baptized again. Cyprian writes to Rome's bishop Stephen, who disagrees. The two churches come close to a break.

step.label: Cyprian, Epistle 71
step.quote: those who have been dipped abroad outside the Church, and have been stained among heretics and schismatics with the taint of profane water
step.note: The heading dates the letter 255. The Church later settled the question differently; Cyprian remains a martyr and saint.

events.text: The emperor Valerian forbids Christian assemblies and begins to exile bishops. Context from settled history.
Cyprian is banished to Curubis, a small town on the coast. His deacon Pontius goes with him.

step.label: Pontius, Life and Passion of Cyprian 11
step.quote: Banishment followed these actions, so good and so benevolent.
step.note: The Notice mentions banishment to Curubis by Valerian; the year 257 comes from the letters associated with it.

events.text: A second edict sentences bishops, priests and deacons to death. Cyprian writes to a fellow bishop that he and his clergy are ready, and that everyone should think less of death than of immortality.

step.label: Cyprian, Epistle 81
step.quote: every one of us may think less of death than of immortality
step.note: The bundled heading says he wrote this near the close of his life, in 258.

events.text: Cyprian is beheaded at Carthage in September. The proconsul's sentence calls him a standard-bearer of the sect and an enemy of the gods. Pontius says he was the first of the African bishops to receive the martyr's crown.

step.label: Pontius, Life and Passion of Cyprian 17
step.quote: a standard-bearer of the sect, and an enemy of the gods
step.note: The Introductory Notice dates his martyrdom to 258; Pontius records the sentence.

name: Perpetua of Carthage
sketch: Vibia Perpetua was a young mother of good family, arrested at Carthage as a catechumen under the persecution of Septimius Severus. She kept a prison diary, the first part of the Passion that bears her name. A friend, Saturus, and an unnamed eyewitness completed it. The year of birth is not known; Butler gives her age as twenty-two, so "c. 181" is only an estimate.

events.text: A group of Christians from Scilli in North Africa is tried at Carthage on 17 July before the proconsul Saturninus, and sentenced to be beheaded. It is among the earliest dated records of African martyrs.

step.label: Passion of the Scillitan Martyrs
step.quote: on the seventeenth day of July, at Carthage
step.note: The text names the consuls but not the year; 180 is the settled date.

events.text: The emperor Severus launches a violent persecution; it reaches Africa the following year.

step.label: Butler, SS. Perpetua and Felicitas
step.quote: A VIOLENT persecution being set on foot by the emperor Severus, in 202, reached Africa the following year
step.note: Butler cites the Acts quoted by Tertullian and Augustine.

events.text: Five catechumens are arrested at Carthage, among them Perpetua, twenty-two, with a baby at the breast, and Felicitas, a slave, who is pregnant.

step.label: Butler, SS. Perpetua and Felicitas
step.quote: Perpetua had an infant at her breast, was of a good family, twenty-two years of age, and married to a person of quality in the city
step.note: Butler adds that her father was a pagan and loved her more than his other children.

events.text: Her father begs her to give up her faith. She asks him if a pot can be called by any other name than what it is, and says she cannot call herself anything but a Christian.

step.label: Perpetua's diary, in Butler
step.quote: Nor can I call myself any other than I am, that is to say, a Christian.
step.note: Butler quotes the part of the Acts that Perpetua wrote herself.

events.text: While still under guard she and her companions receive baptism. She prays only for patience under bodily pain.

step.label: Perpetua's diary, in Butler
step.quote: after this we enjoyed a little repose, and in that interval received baptism
step.note: She writes that the Holy Spirit moved her to ask only for patience.

events.text: They are moved into prison. She is shocked by the darkness and the crowd. She is also tortured by worry for her baby, until the deacons pay for her to nurse him.

step.label: Perpetua's diary, in Butler
step.quote: I was shocked at the horror and darkness of the place; for till then I knew not what such sort of places were.
step.note: She writes that after a few days her prison itself seemed agreeable.

events.text: She asks to know whether she will be martyred. She sees a vision of a golden ladder to heaven guarded by a dragon, and she and her brother understand that she will die.

step.label: Perpetua's diary, in Butler
step.quote: I saw a golden ladder which reached from earth to the heavens
step.note: The first of her four recorded visions.

events.text: At the trial the governor Hilarian urges her to sacrifice for the emperor, and her father appears with her child. She says "Yes, I am" a Christian. The sentence is wild beasts in the games.

step.label: Perpetua's diary, in Butler
step.quote: Then the judge pronounced our sentence, by which we were all condemned to be exposed to wild beasts.
step.note: The proconsul had just died, so the procurator Hilarian presided.

events.text: She prays for her dead little brother Dinocrates and sees him in a vision healed and refreshed. She understands that her prayer has relieved his suffering.

step.label: Perpetua's diary, in Butler
step.quote: I awoke, and I knew he was relieved from his pain.
step.note: Butler includes the whole vision from her diary.

events.text: In labor in prison, Felicitas is told she will not be able to bear the beasts if she cannot bear childbirth. She answers that another will suffer in her.

step.label: Butler, SS. Perpetua and Felicitas
step.quote: It is I that suffer what I now suffer; but then there will be another in me that will suffer for me, because I shall suffer for him.
step.note: Her daughter is raised by a Christian woman. This part of the Acts was written by the eyewitness.

events.text: On the eve of the games she dreams that she is wrestling an Egyptian in the amphitheatre and wins. She understands the fight is not with beasts but with the devil.

step.label: Perpetua's diary, in Butler
step.quote: found that I was not so much to combat with wild beasts as with the devils.
step.note: This is the last entry she wrote.

events.text: On 7 March they are led into the arena. Perpetua is tossed by a wild cow, helps Felicitas to her feet, and dies by the sword of an inexperienced gladiator.

step.label: Butler, SS. Perpetua and Felicitas
step.quote: The day of their martyrdom was the 7th of March
step.note: Butler says the most ancient martyrologies and the Roman calendar of 354 mark that day.

events.text: More than a century and a half later, the feast of Perpetua and Felicitas is listed in the Roman calendar of 354, and the saints are named in the canon of the Mass. Augustine says their feast drew more people every year.

step.label: Butler, SS. Perpetua and Felicitas
step.quote: They are mentioned in the canon of the Mass.
step.note: Butler cites Augustine's sermons on their feast.

name: Ignatius of Antioch
sketch: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch in Syria. We know almost nothing of his life before he was arrested and sent to Rome to die. His seven letters, written on the road, are among the earliest Christian writings after the New Testament. The year of his death is disputed (107 or 116), so every date here after 98 is approximate.

events.text: The Romans destroy Jerusalem and the Temple. Antioch, where followers of Jesus were first called Christians, becomes a leading centre of the Church. Context from settled history.

Ignatius becomes the second bishop of Antioch. Eusebius's Chronicle dates his episcopate from about 69-72, which the editor of the bundled text judges unreliable. All that is secure is that he held the see.

step.label: Eusebius, Church History III.36, editor's note
step.quote: that Ignatius was second bishop of Antioch
step.note: The note says this is the earliest report, and that nothing reliable is known about his life apart from his martyrdom.

events.text: Trajan becomes emperor; the persecution under him is the setting for Ignatius's arrest.

step.label: Martyrdom of Ignatius
step.quote: The date of Trajan's accession was a.d. 98.
step.note: A note in the bundled text gives the date of the accession.

events.text: Condemned for being a Christian, Ignatius is taken from Antioch to the port of Seleucia and shipped toward Rome under guard.

step.label: Martyrdom of Ignatius
step.quote: he came down from Antioch to Seleucia, from which place he set sail
step.note: The notes say the date is either 107 or 116, depending on the reading of the emperor's regnal year. The account itself is of disputed date and authorship.

events.text: At Smyrna he is welcomed by its bishop Polycarp, whom tradition says was his fellow-disciple of St. John.

step.label: Martyrdom of Ignatius
step.quote: hastened to see the holy Polycarp, [formerly] his fellow-disciple, and [now] bishop of Smyrna
step.note: The Introductory Note calls the common discipleship under John a tradition not inconsistent with anything in the letters.

events.text: Guarded by soldiers, he stops at cities along the way, encouraging each church, warning against false teaching and urging them to hold fast to the tradition of the apostles.

step.label: Eusebius, Church History III.36
step.quote: he fortified the parishes in the various cities where he stopped by oral homilies and exhortations
step.note: Eusebius is the earliest narrator after Polycarp and Irenaeus.

events.text: From Smyrna he writes to the churches at Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles, and to the Christians of Rome. Later, from Troas, he writes to Philadelphia, to Smyrna and to Polycarp.

step.label: Eusebius, Church History III.36
step.quote: So when he came to Smyrna, where Polycarp was, he wrote an epistle to the church of Ephesus
step.note: The editor lists seven genuine letters in two groups, four from Smyrna and three from Troas.

events.text: He begs the Roman Christians not to save him by influence. He asks to be allowed to die, comparing himself to wheat ground by the teeth of beasts.

step.label: Ignatius, Letter to the Romans
step.quote: Suffer me to become food for the wild beasts, through whose instrumentality it will be granted me to attain to God.
step.note: The same sentence appears in both the shorter and longer versions in the bundled text.

events.text: He tells Polycarp to hold firm against teachers who seem trustworthy but teach strange doctrine.

step.label: Ignatius, Letter to Polycarp (Syriac)
step.quote: stand thou in the truth, as an athlete
step.note: The Greek, as the bundled note says, has "like an anvil" here.

events.text: He is brought into the amphitheatre at Rome and killed by wild beasts, according to the late account of his martyrdom, on 20 December. The eyewitness claim in that account is disputed.

step.label: Martyrdom of Ignatius
step.quote: Now these things took place on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, that is, on the twentieth of December
step.note: The Introductory Note says no reference to this narrative is found in the first six centuries, so treat the details with caution. The Greeks still keep 20 December.

events.text: Polycarp writes to the Philippians, holding up Ignatius and others as examples of patient endurance.

step.label: Polycarp, Letter to the Philippians 9
step.quote: not only in the case of the blessed Ignatius, and Zosimus, and Rufus
step.note: This letter is the earliest outside witness to Ignatius.

name: Martin of Tours
sketch: Martin was the son of a Roman army officer, a soldier who became a monk and then, against his will, bishop of Tours. His friend Sulpitius Severus wrote his life while he was still living, and Butler follows it. Several of the wonders told of him are legend-like; this timeline keeps to the events Sulpitius and Butler date or place in his life.

events.text: Martin is born at Sabaria in Pannonia (modern Hungary), the son of a pagan army officer, and grows up in Pavia in Italy.

step.label: Butler, St. Martin of Tours
step.quote: St. Gregory of Tours places his birth in the year 316, or before Easter in 317, the eleventh of Constantine the Great.
step.note: Butler gives the year as 316 or early 317.

events.text: At fifteen he is forced by an imperial order to take the military oath and is enrolled in the cavalry, though he already wanted the monastic life.

step.label: Butler, St. Martin of Tours
step.quote: at fifteen years of age he was compelled to take the military oath, and was entered in the cavalry
step.note: The year follows from his birth year; Butler does not give it.

events.text: At the gate of Amiens in a hard winter, he cuts his cloak in two and gives half to a naked beggar. That night he sees Christ wearing the half-cloak.

step.label: Butler, St. Martin of Tours
step.quote: he met at the gate of the city of Amiens a poor man, almost naked, trembling and shaking for cold
step.note: The year is an estimate. Sulpitius says he was baptized soon after.

events.text: As the barbarians press into Gaul under Julian the Caesar, Martin asks to leave the army, saying he is a soldier of Christ.

step.label: Sulpitius Severus, Life of St. Martin 4
step.quote: as the barbarians were rushing within the two divisions of Gaul, Julian Cæsar
step.note: The chapter is cut short in the bundled text. The date is an estimate from Julian's command in Gaul.

events.text: He joins Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, who wants to ordain him a deacon. Martin's humility refuses; he accepts only the minor order of exorcist.

step.label: Butler, St. Martin of Tours
step.quote: was obliged to be content only to make him exorcist
step.note: Butler says Hilary became bishop of Poitiers in 353 or 354.

events.text: In Illyricum he opposes the Arians so strongly that he is publicly whipped and driven out of the city. Hilary himself is banished.

step.label: Sulpitius Severus, Life of St. Martin 6
step.quote: he was publicly scourged, and at last was compelled to leave the city
step.note: The date is approximate. The same chapter tells how the devil said he would resist him wherever he went.

events.text: Julian becomes sole emperor and tries to restore the old worship. Context from settled history.
Reunited with Hilary, Martin founds a monastery a short distance from Poitiers, the first in Gaul.

step.label: Sulpitius Severus, Life of St. Martin 7
step.quote: he established for himself a monastery not far from the town
step.note: The year is the usual estimate; Sulpitius does not give it.

events.text: The people of Tours demand him as bishop. He is consecrated on 3 July 371, and Butler says he accepted it reluctantly.

step.label: Butler, St. Martin of Tours
step.quote: in the year 371 he was chosen the third bishop of Tours, and consecrated on the 3d of July
step.note: Butler gives the date.

events.text: As bishop he keeps the same humble habits and the same plain clothes, and builds a monastery two miles from the city so that he can keep the solitude of a hermit.

step.label: Sulpitius Severus, Life of St. Martin 10
step.quote: he established a monastery for himself about two miles outside the city
step.note: This is the monastery later called Marmoutier.

events.text: He doubts a local shrine said to hold martyrs and asks the clergy for the martyr's name and date. When none can be given, he stops the veneration there.

step.label: Sulpitius Severus, Life of St. Martin 11
step.quote: Martin, not inclined to give a hasty belief to things uncertain
step.note: The date is approximate; the story belongs to his early years as bishop.

events.text: Tearing down temples in the countryside, he is attacked by a pagan with a sword. Martin bares his neck, and the man falls and begs pardon.

step.label: Sulpitius Severus, Life of St. Martin 15
step.quote: Martin, throwing back his cloak, offered his bare neck to the assassin
step.note: Sulpitius gives no year. The chapter is about his mission to the villages.

events.text: He refuses to dine with the usurper Maximus, who had killed an emperor, and speaks to him as a bishop speaks to a king. Later he pleads against the execution of Priscillian and his followers.

step.label: Sulpitius Severus, Life of St. Martin 20
step.quote: in Martin alone, apostolic authority continued to assert itself
step.note: Dates for Maximus's reign are 383-388; the year here is an estimate.

events.text: Martin knows his death is near and sets out to visit the church at Condate (the name the text gives the place) and dies there. Sulpitius describes it in a letter to his mother-in-law.

step.label: Sulpitius Severus, Letter 3 to Bassula
step.quote: Martin was aware of the period of his own death long before it occurred
step.note: Butler gives 397 for his death.

name: The Venerable Bede
sketch: Bede was given to a monastery at seven and never really left it. In the twin houses of Wearmouth and Jarrow in Northumbria he read, taught and wrote: Scripture commentary, saints' lives, a work on time and the Church History of the English People. He is the only English Doctor of the Church.

events.text: Augustine of Canterbury lands in Kent and begins the mission to the English, which Bede tells in Book 1 of his History.

step.label: Bede, Ecclesiastical History I.25
step.quote: How Augustine, coming into Britain, first preached in the Isle
step.note: The chapter heading carries the date 597.

events.text: The Synod of Whitby settles the dispute over the date of Easter in the Northumbrian church in favour of the Roman reckoning. Bede tells the story in Book 3. Context from settled history.
Bede is born in 673 in the lands that soon belong to the new monastery of Wearmouth, founded in 674.

step.label: Butler, Venerable Bede
step.quote: was born in 673, as Mabillon demonstrates from his own writings
step.note: Butler follows Mabillon for the year.

events.text: At seven he is handed over by his kinsmen to Abbot Benedict Biscop to be educated, and later to Ceolfrid. The sister house of Jarrow is founded in 680.

step.label: Bede, Ecclesiastical History V.24
step.quote: I was given, by the care of kinsmen, at seven years of age, to be educated by the most reverend Abbot Benedict
step.note: The year follows from his birth year; Butler dates the founding of Jarrow to 680.

events.text: He spends the rest of his life as a monk of Wearmouth and Jarrow, keeping the round of services and the learning.

step.label: Bede, Ecclesiastical History V.24
step.quote: I always took delight in learning, or teaching, or writing
step.note: He writes this in the last chapter of his History.

events.text: He is ordained deacon at nineteen, a little early, because of his learning and holiness.

step.label: Butler, Venerable Bede
step.quote: he was ordained deacon in 691, at nineteen years of age
step.note: Bede himself says he was ordained deacon in his nineteenth year.

events.text: At thirty he is ordained priest and begins his long series of commentaries compiled from the Fathers.

step.label: Butler, Venerable Bede
step.quote: at thirty years of age, in 702, he was ordained priest
step.note: Butler again follows Bede's own statement.

events.text: In his fifty-ninth year he finishes the Ecclesiastical History and lists his own writings at the end of it.

step.label: Bede, Ecclesiastical History V.24
step.quote: From the time when I received priest's orders, till the fifty-ninth year of my age
step.note: 59 years from 673 is 731-732. This is the traditional date of completion.

events.text: He writes a letter of advice to Egbert, his former pupil, on Egbert's becoming archbishop of York.

step.label: Butler, Venerable Bede
step.quote: lived long enough to write him a letter of advice upon his advancement
step.note: Butler dates Egbert's consecration to 734.

events.text: Two weeks before Easter his breathing grows labored, but he stays cheerful, giving thanks day and night, and keeps teaching.

step.label: Butler, Venerable Bede
step.quote: He began to be much troubled with a shortness of breath about two weeks before Easter, yet without pain
step.note: This comes from the letter of his pupil Cuthbert, which Butler summarises.

events.text: He keeps dictating a translation of the Gospel of John and of notes from Isidore, saying he will not leave his pupils a falsehood to read after his death.

step.label: Butler, Venerable Bede
step.quote: I will not have my scholars read a falsehood after my death, and labor without advantage
step.note: Cuthbert reports the words.

events.text: Bede dies on 26 May 735, the eve of the Ascension, lying on the floor of his cell and praying the Holy Spirit.

step.label: Butler, Venerable Bede
step.quote: Bede died in the year 735, of his age sixty-two
step.note: Butler gives the date as the evening of Wednesday, 26 May 735.

events.text: In 1020 his remains are carried to Durham and laid in the shrine of St. Cuthbert.

step.label: Butler, Venerable Bede
step.quote: In 1020 his sacred remains were conveyed to Durham
step.note: Butler adds that they were later enclosed in a richer shrine in 1155.
